Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: Memory usage grows by 4·N·C·H·W bytes per iteration due to the allocation of the linear layer's output; with COMMIT_ADAPTIVE the command buffer is not committed until low‑memory conditions arise, so the buffers accumulate, while COMMIT_AND_WAIT forces immediate commits and frees the memory.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Including the example from @bashtage's PR that demonstrates broadcasting with `rng.multinomial` and the resulting output shape.

original_statement: It turns out this was a difference in inflate/deflate implementations between the extension/SDK and the CLI. The SDK uses Node's zlib bindings, while by default Rust's flate2 library uses a rust port of miniz. miniz does not appear to flush decompressed data as nicely on SYNC'd boundaries as zlib does, which caused data to 'stall'. This could also be the cause of some connection flakiness!
rephrased_statement: The discrepancy originates from divergent inflate/deflate back‑ends: the SDK leverages Node's native zlib bindings, whereas the CLI defaults to Rust's flate2, which wraps a miniz port. Miniz's block‑aligned flushing semantics diverge from zlib's, leading to residual buffers and intermittent stalls, potentially manifesting as connection instability.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: The observed memory behavior is a known trade-off in MPS's adaptive commit model: by deferring command buffer submission, we optimize GPU utilization at the cost of delayed buffer reclamation. Your nn.Linear loop generates output tensors that persist until either (a) the buffer is flushed by memory pressure, or (b) Python’s GC runs due to reference count dropping to zero. Since you're not storing outputs, the latter depends on interpreter internals. This is correct, albeit unintuitive. Recommend users who need deterministic memory behavior to opt into COMMIT_AND_WAIT or use context managers to force scope exit.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.
rephrased_statement: From the NCCL team's perspective, the function ncclCommGetAsyncError has historically been implemented as a pure read‑only call; while the API never officially promised read‑only semantics, the source code up to NCCL 2.25 behaved exactly that way. In NCCL 2.26 we introduced a modification to address a subtle race condition that could arise during the cleanup of asynchronous operations launched by non‑blocking communicators. The fix adds a tiny amount of internal housekeeping to the routine, so that invoking ncclCommGetAsyncError now not only retrieves the current error status but also may perform a brief cleanup of pending work. This change eliminates the race, but it also means the function is no longer a strict read‑only operation as it once was.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: SciPy development includes updates to existing multivariate distributions and addition of new ones, with a goal of maintaining consistency with NumPy's multivariate distribution behavior.

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken

  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)

>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works

Starting with the 2.26 release we introduced a change that addresses a race condition observed when non‑blocking communicators finish their work and are cleaned up. The updated implementation now performs a minimal cleanup of pending asynchronous operations before returning the error code. As a result, the routine can modify internal state, which is a deliberate design decision to ensure correctness in the presence of concurrent cleanup tasks.

original_statement: It turns out this was a difference in inflate/deflate implementations between the extension/SDK and the CLI. The SDK uses Node's zlib bindings, while by default Rust's flate2 library uses a rust port of miniz. miniz does not appear to flush decompressed data as nicely on SYNC'd boundaries as zlib does, which caused data to 'stall'. This could also be the cause of some connection flakiness!

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: SciPy is extending its multivariate distribution implementations and aims to keep behavior aligned with NumPy's multivariate distributions.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.
rephrased_statement: According to the NCCL development team, the historical behavior of ncclCommGetAsyncError was that of a read‑only query; while the API never explicitly guaranteed read‑only semantics, the underlying code up to version 2.25 never performed any side‑effects. In the 2.26 release we made a targeted change to eliminate a race condition that could occur during the cleanup phase of asynchronous operations launched by non‑blocking communicators. The modification adds a small amount of cleanup work to the function, so that invoking ncclCommGetAsyncError now both fetches the current error status and may tidy up lingering asynchronous state. This resolves the concurrency issue but also means the function is no longer a pure read operation as it once was.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.
rephrased_statement: The NCCL team clarifies: while ncclCommGetAsyncError was *de facto* a read-only function before 2.26, it now has a side effect — triggering light cleanup during error checks — to resolve a known race condition in nonblocking communicators. This behavior is intentional and documented in the release notes.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: The interaction between the `size` argument and broadcasting of distribution parameters (which may be 1‑D or 2‑D arrays) is being examined.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: Thanks for waiting, @hvaara – after instrumenting the metal‑resource trace I believe the memory increase per iteration is roughly 4 × N × C × H × W bytes, i.e. the size of the Linear layer's output allocated at L50. When `executeMPSGraph` runs with `SyncMode::COMMIT_ADAPTIVE`, the operation is recorded into the active MPSStream command buffer but, unless the device hits a high‑memory pressure state, the buffer is not flushed, causing subsequent iterations to reuse the same buffer. Since each `nn.Linear` call must keep its output tensor alive until the Python reference disappears, the memory usage climbs while the command buffer accumulates more encoded work. Switching to `COMMIT_AND_WAIT` forces a buffer commit after each encode, which should allow the runtime to release the output buffers once the call finishes, thereby giving the GC a chance to collect the Python objects (we never bind the results). I validated this by letting the adaptive commit run its course, then sleeping about 5‑6 seconds, after which the memory usage dropped. In real code, periodic synchronizations would likely trigger similar reclamation. Consequently, my provisional assessment is that the observed memory pattern is expected; the opacity of `COMMIT_ADAPTIVE` arises from its device‑specific commit policy and the timing of Python‑level garbage collection. Let me know if this interpretation seems reasonable or if we missed something.

original_statement:
Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: In COMMIT_ADAPTIVE SyncMode, operations are encoded into the active MPSStream command buffer without immediate commitment unless memory pressure thresholds are reached.

rephrased_statement: Hey @hvaara, thanks for hanging in there! I poked around the metal‑resource traces and figured out why memory keeps climbing: each loop allocates a new output tensor from the linear layer (4 × N × C × H × W bytes). With COMMIT_ADAPTIVE we keep stuffing ops into the same MPS command buffer until memory pressure forces a commit, so those tensors hang around until the Python objects are GC’d. Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.

    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.
rephrased_statement: To provide some context from the NCCL perspective: historically, ncclCommGetAsyncError acted as a read‑only query (without any formal guarantee of such behavior). With the advent of NCCL 2.26, the function was updated to occasionally carry out a small cleanup task, a change introduced to resolve a race condition observed during the cleanup phase of asynchronous operations issued by non‑blocking communicators.

original_statement: It turns out this was a difference in inflate/deflate implementations between the extension/SDK and the CLI. The SDK uses Node's zlib bindings, while by default Rust's flate2 library uses a rust port of miniz. miniz does not appear to flush decompressed data as nicely on SYNC'd boundaries as zlib does, which caused data to 'stall'. This could also be the cause of some connection flakiness!
rephrased_statement: What we discovered is that the SDK and the CLI aren't using the same compression library. The SDK calls Node's zlib, but the CLI defaults to the Rust flate2 crate (a miniz port). Miniz tends to leave partially decompressed buffers unflushed at SYNC points, leading to data stalls and occasional connection instability.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.
rephrased_statement: Historically, ncclCommGetAsyncError behaved as a read-only operation in prior NCCL versions, though this was not an explicit guarantee.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: Thanks for waiting, @hvaara! I’ve been looking at the metal resource logs and here’s my current take: each loop iteration creates a linear‑layer output of size 4 × N × C × H × W bytes, which explains the steady memory increase; when we run with COMMIT_ADAPTIVE the MPSStream keeps appending ops to the same command buffer until the GPU’s low‑memory watermark triggers a commit, so we don’t see immediate releases; the nn.Linear output tensor stays alive until Python’s garbage collector finally runs, so memory keeps climbing while the buffer fills. Switching to COMMIT_AND_WAIT forces a commit after each encode, freeing the buffers right away and letting the GC clean up since we never keep a reference to the result. I tweaked the script to let the adaptive commit finish and waited about 5‑6 seconds, and the memory was reclaimed. Bottom line: the memory pattern looks intentional, but COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit hidden because its commit timing is device‑dependent and also tied to when Python actually collects the objects. Does that sound reasonable, or is there a symptom we’re missing?

Each iteration allocates a linear layer output of 4 × N × C × H × W bytes, and with COMMIT_ADAPTIVE the MPS command buffer accumulates these operations without committing until the device’s low‑memory watermark is reached, which keeps the output buffers alive. Switching to COMMIT_AND_WAIT forces a commit after every encode, allowing the Python garbage collector to reclaim the tensors immediately. My test, which added a short wait (≈5 seconds) to let the adaptive commit finish, showed the memory being released as expected. Thus, the current memory management is correct; the only downside is that COMMIT_ADAPTIVE’s lazy commit makes memory usage appear erratic.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.
rephrased_statement: As of NCCL 2.26, ncclCommGetAsyncError is no longer a passive status checker. To address race conditions in nonblocking communicator cleanup, it now includes light cleanup logic during error polling—a behavior change that aligns with formal guarantees but breaks assumptions built on its previous read-only implementation.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: Feedback is requested on whether the observed behavior aligns with expected system design or if it indicates a need for adjustment in adaptive commit logic.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Reference gufunc signatures for existing multivariate distributions (e.g., dirichlet: (n)->(n), multinomial: (),(n)->(n), multivariate_normal: (n),(n,n)->(n), multivariate_hypergeometric: (n),()->(n)) are listed for context.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)
rephrased_statement: Seen a similar pattern with a `polars.Series` object: `np.mean(a)` raises `TypeError` because `Series.mean()` does not accept the `axis` keyword argument, while `np.mean(np.asarray(a))` works as expected.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.

original_statement:
Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.
rephrased_statement: The benchmark uses torch.no_grad() and the nightly PyTorch build compiled from source (v1.11.0).

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Reference gufunc signatures for current multivariate distributions are provided, e.g., `dirichlet(alpha) -> (n)`, `multinomial(n, pvals) -> (n)`, `multivariate_normal(mean, cov) -> (n)`, and `multivariate_hypergeometric(colors, nsample) -> (n)`.

original_statement:
Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: What's up @hvaara, thanks for hanging on! I pulled the metal resource logs and here's the lowdown: each iteration spits out a linear layer tensor (size = 4·N·C·H·W bytes), so memory climbs by that chunk. With `COMMIT_ADAPTIVE` the MPS stream keeps stuffing ops into one command buffer and only flushes when the device gets low on memory, which means those output buffers stick around. Flip to `COMMIT_AND_WAIT` and the buffer gets committed after every step, letting Python’s GC clean up the tensors right away because we never assign them. I let the adaptive version sit idle for about 5–6 seconds and the memory was released, confirming the theory. Bottom line: memory management is fine; it just looks weird because adaptive commits are hidden behind the device’s watermark.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.
rephrased_statement: If you're relying on ncclCommGetAsyncError being side-effect-free, be aware: since NCCL 2.26, it can trigger cleanup logic during error checks, especially with nonblocking comms. This wasn’t the case before — it was accidentally read-only.

original_statement:
Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: The current behavior of COMMIT_ADAPTIVE may appear non-deterministic to users due to opaque trigger conditions tied to device memory pressure.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: A pull request by @bashtage adds broadcasting support to `rng.multinomial`; the example creates a 4 × 2 broadcast of `n` and `pvals` and draws 10 variates per combination, resulting in an output shape of (10, 4, 2, 3).

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.
rephrased_statement: Benchmark on a MacBook M1: CPU 18.38 s vs. MPS 36.00 s for batch size 64 using `BertForSequenceClassification` (see code snippet below).

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.
rephrased_statement: According to the NCCL developers, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, until the 2.26 release, essentially a read‑only accessor (as @ptrblck noted), with no formal guarantee of being side‑effect‑free. The 2.26 update added a cleanup mechanism to address a race condition in the teardown of async operations from non‑blocking communicators—referencing @lw's comment—so the call may now perform some internal cleanup while returning the error flag.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.
rephrased_statement: In NCCL versions prior to 2.26, ncclCommGetAsyncError performed only a read of the error status; it was not designed to modify any internal state, although this was not a documented guarantee.

rephrased_statement: In this update we’re fixing a subtle but annoying type mismatch in the Cython bindings for NumPy’s iterator API. The function `NpyIter_GetIterNext` was declared to return a pointer (`NpyIter_IterNextFunc*`), but the underlying C implementation actually returns the function type itself (`NpyIter_IterNextFunc`). This discrepancy caused Cython to generate invalid code, leading to compile‑time failures for anyone trying to use the iterator’s next‑function from Cython. The patch simply swaps the return annotation to the correct type, which clears the compilation errors and aligns the Cython wrapper with the real NumPy signature.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up.
